section.title: Israel Settles in Egypt
section.sectionRationale: The whole household of Jacob goes down to Egypt, but not before God meets Jacob at Beersheba with a promise to go with him. A careful roll of names records the seed that will become a nation, father and son are reunited, and Israel is settled and multiplied in Goshen even as Egypt itself passes into Pharaoh's hand.
section.thesis: God confirms His covenant as He brings Israel down to Egypt, providing through Joseph so that the family becomes fruitful in Goshen while Jacob looks beyond his death to the land of promise.
section.frameNote: Six scenes: God's word at Beersheba; the roll of those who went to Egypt; the reunion of father and son; the audience with Pharaoh and settlement in Goshen; the famine years and the land of Egypt; and Israel's growth with Jacob's charge to be buried with his fathers.

units.label: God speaks at Beersheba
units.note: do not be afraid to go down to Egypt

verses.text: So Israel set out with all that he had, and when he came to Beersheba, he offered {{zevach|sacrifices}} to the God of his father Isaac.
And that night God spoke to Israel in a {{marah|vision}}: “Jacob, Jacob!” He said. “Here I am,” replied Jacob.
“I am God,” He said, “the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make you into a great {{goy|nation}} there.
I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will surely bring you back. And Joseph’s own hands will close your eyes.”
Then Jacob departed from Beersheba, and the sons of Israel took their father Jacob in the wagons Pharaoh had sent to carry him, along with their children and wives.
They also took the livestock and possessions they had acquired in the land of Canaan, and Jacob and all his offspring went to Egypt.
Jacob took with him to Egypt his sons and grandsons, and his daughters and granddaughters, all his offspring.
Now these are the names of the sons of Israel (Jacob and his descendants) who went to Egypt: Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn.
The sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanite woman.
The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah; but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. The sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul.
The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Job, and Shimron.
The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.
These are the sons of Leah born to Jacob in Paddan-aram, in addition to his daughter Dinah. The total number of sons and daughters was thirty-three.
The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.
The children of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and their sister Serah. The sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel.
These are the sons of Jacob born to Zilpah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Leah, sixteen in all.
The sons of Jacob’s wife Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.
Manasseh and Ephraim were born to Joseph in the land of Egypt by Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On.
The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.
These are the sons of Rachel born to Jacob, fourteen in all.
The son of Dan: Hushim.
The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
These are the sons of Jacob born to Bilhah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel, seven in all.
All those belonging to Jacob who came to Egypt, his direct descendants, besides the wives of Jacob’s sons, numbered sixty-six persons.
And with the two sons who had been born to Joseph in Egypt, the members of Jacob’s family who went to Egypt were seventy in all.

units.label: Father and son reunited
units.note: finally I can die, now that I have seen your face

verses.text: Now Jacob had sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to get directions to Goshen. When Jacob’s family arrived in the land of Goshen,
Joseph prepared his chariot and went there to meet his father Israel. Joseph presented himself to him, embraced him, and wept profusely.
Then Israel said to Joseph, “Finally I can die, now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive!”
Joseph said to his brothers and to his father’s household, “I will go up and inform Pharaoh: ‘My brothers and my father’s household from the land of Canaan have come to me.
The men are shepherds; they raise livestock, and they have brought their flocks and herds and all that they own.’
When Pharaoh summons you and asks, ‘What is your occupation?’

you are to say, ‘Your servants have raised livestock ever since our youth, both we and our fathers.’ Then you will be allowed to settle in the land of Goshen, since all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians.”
So Joseph went and told Pharaoh: “My father and my brothers, with their flocks and herds and all they own, have come from the land of Canaan and are now in Goshen.”
And he chose five of his brothers and presented them before Pharaoh.
“What is your occupation?” Pharaoh asked Joseph’s brothers. “Your servants are shepherds,” they replied, “both we and our fathers.”

Then they said to Pharaoh, “We have come to live in the land for a time, because there is no pasture for the flocks of your servants, since the famine in the land of Canaan has been severe. So now, please allow your servants to settle in the land of Goshen.”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Now that your father and brothers have come to you,

the land of Egypt is before you; settle your father and brothers in the best part of the land. They may dwell in the land of Goshen. And if you know of any talented men among them, put them in charge of my own livestock.”
Then Joseph brought in his father Jacob and presented him before Pharaoh, and Jacob {{barak|blessed}} Pharaoh.
“How many years have you lived?” Pharaoh asked.
“My travels have lasted 130 years,” Jacob replied. “My years have been few and hard, and they have not matched the years of the travels of my fathers.”
Then Jacob blessed Pharaoh and departed from his presence.
So Joseph settled his father and brothers in the land of Egypt and gave them property in the best part of the land, the district of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded.
Joseph also provided his father and brothers and all his father’s household with food for their families.

units.label: The famine and the land of Egypt

verses.text: There was no food, however, in all that region, because the famine was so severe; the lands of Egypt and Canaan had been exhausted by the famine.
Joseph collected all the money to be found in the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan in exchange for the grain they were buying, and he brought it into Pharaoh’s palace.
When the money from the lands of Egypt and Canaan was gone, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and said, “Give us food. Why should we die before your eyes? For our funds have run out!”
“Then bring me your livestock,” said Joseph. “Since the money is gone, I will sell you food in exchange for your livestock.”

So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and he gave them food in exchange for their horses, their flocks and herds, and their donkeys. Throughout that year he provided them with food in exchange for all their livestock.

When that year was over, they came to him the second year and said, “We cannot hide from our lord that our money is gone and all our livestock belongs to you. There is nothing left for our lord except our bodies and our land.

Why should we perish before your eyes, we and our land as well? Purchase us and our land in exchange for food. Then we, along with our land, will be slaves to Pharaoh. Give us seed that we may live and not die, and that the land may not become desolate.”
So Joseph acquired for Pharaoh all the land in Egypt; the Egyptians, one and all, sold their fields because the famine was so severe upon them. The land became Pharaoh’s,
and Joseph reduced the people to servitude from one end of Egypt to the other.
However, he did not acquire the priests’ portion of the land, for it had been given to them by Pharaoh. They ate the rations that Pharaoh supplied; so they did not sell their land.
Then Joseph said to the people, “Now that I have acquired you and your land for Pharaoh this day, here is seed for you to sow in the land.
At harvest time, you are to give a fifth of it to Pharaoh, and four-fifths will be yours as seed for the field and food for yourselves and your households and children.”
“You have saved our lives,” they said. “We have found favor in our lord’s eyes, and we will be Pharaoh’s servants.”
So Joseph established a law that a fifth of the produce belongs to Pharaoh, and it is in effect in the land of Egypt to this day. Only the priests’ land does not belong to Pharaoh.

units.label: Israel grows; Jacob's charge
units.note: do not bury me in Egypt

verses.text: Now the Israelites settled in the land of Egypt, in the region of Goshen. They acquired property there and became fruitful and increased greatly in number.
And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years, and the length of his life was 147 years.

When the time drew near for Israel to die, he called his son Joseph and said to him, “If I have found favor in your eyes, put your hand under my thigh and promise to show me kindness and faithfulness. Do not bury me in Egypt,
but when I lie down with my fathers, carry me out of Egypt and bury me with them.” Joseph answered, “I will do as you have requested.”
“Swear to me,” Jacob said. So Joseph swore to him, and Israel bowed in worship at the head of his bed.

zevach.gloss: A sacrifice, especially an animal offered to God. At the border of the promised land Jacob pauses to worship before going down to Egypt. The sacrifice frames the whole journey as an act of faith seeking God's direction.

marah.gloss: A vision, a revelatory appearance in which God makes Himself known. God meets Jacob by night in such a vision, calling his name and renewing the covenant. It marks a turning point, God's own approval of the descent into Egypt.

goy.gloss: A nation or people. God promises to make Jacob into a great nation in Egypt, echoing the pledge to Abraham. The word looks ahead to Israel's growth from a household of seventy into a mighty people.

barak.gloss: To bless, to speak good and favor over another. The aged patriarch, a mere resident alien, blesses the mighty Pharaoh, and the lesser is blessed by the greater. It quietly signals whose God is truly sovereign in the encounter.

basic.context: Jacob moves his entire family to Egypt, but first God meets him at Beersheba and promises to go with him. A roll of seventy names records the family that will become a nation, Joseph and Jacob are reunited, and Israel settles in Goshen. The key question is whether leaving the promised land means leaving the promise behind.
basic.hermeneutics: This is narrative with an embedded genealogy and a royal audience. The main question is how to read the descent into Egypt: is it a detour or part of God's plan? God's word in the vision settles it, this is His doing, and He will bring them back.
basic.originalLanguages: Jacob offers zevach, sacrifices, and God appears in a marah, a vision, promising to make him a great goy, nation. Later the aged Jacob speaks barak, blessing, over Pharaoh, the lesser blessing the greater, hinting who truly holds authority.
basic.typology: Israel goes down into Egypt and will one day be brought up again, a pattern the exodus fulfills and the Gospels echo when the child Jesus is called out of Egypt. Joseph's provision of bread and land foreshadows Christ's provision for His people.
basic.christ: Joseph sustains a starving world and gathers his family to safety, a picture of Christ who feeds the hungry and gathers His people. Jacob's dying insistence on burial in the promised land looks in hope beyond death to God's promise, fulfilled in the resurrection Christ secures.
basic.god: God promises, I will go down with you and I will surely bring you back. He is present with His people even in a foreign land and faithful to His covenant across generations. Behind Joseph's administration stands God's providence keeping Israel alive.
basic.crossReferences: The seventy who went down grow into the nation of Exodus 1. The promise to bring them back is fulfilled in the exodus, and Hebrews 11 commends Jacob's faith as he blesses and worships at his death.
basic.oneStory: The family of promise becomes a nation in Egypt, exactly as God said. The descent is not the end of the covenant but a chapter in it, setting up the exodus and, far ahead, the coming of the Saviour from this people.

context.literary:
These two chapters are framed by worship. They open with Israel offering sacrifices at Beersheba, Genesis 46:1, and close with Israel bowing in worship at the head of his bed, Genesis 47:31. Between those two acts the whole family moves from Canaan to Egypt, but the frame tells the reader that the move is to be understood before God.

The night vision of Genesis 46:2-4 is the last time God speaks directly to a patriarch in Genesis. Its form recalls earlier calls: the doubled name, 'Jacob, Jacob,' and the answer, 'Here I am,' as with 'Abraham, Abraham' on Moriah, Genesis 22:11. Its content gathers up the promises of the book: a great nation, Genesis 12:2, the presence of God, Genesis 28:15, and a return to the land.

The list of names, Genesis 46:8-27, opens with a formula that Exodus repeats almost word for word, 'These are the names of the sons of Israel who went to Egypt,' Exodus 1:1. The list is ordered by the four mothers, Leah, Zilpah, Rachel and Bilhah, with subtotals of thirty three, sixteen, fourteen and seven, which together make seventy. The list quietly includes the sorrows of the story: Er and Onan who died in Canaan, verse 12, and Shaul 'the son of a Canaanite woman,' verse 10.

The narrative then moves through a reunion, verses 28 to 30, a coached audience, Genesis 46:31 to 47:6, and Jacob's own audience, Genesis 47:7-10, which begins and ends with Jacob blessing Pharaoh. The account of the famine policy, Genesis 47:13-26, reads at first like a digression, but it sets up a pointed contrast. The Egyptians sell their livestock, their land and themselves to Pharaoh; the Israelites are given property, Genesis 47:11, and 'acquired property there and became fruitful,' Genesis 47:27. The last scene, Genesis 47:28-31, turns to Jacob's death and to the land beyond Egypt, preparing for the blessings of chapters 48 and 49.
context.historical:
Beersheba stood at the southern edge of Canaan, the last settled place on the road toward Egypt. It carried family memory. Abraham planted a tamarisk there and called on the LORD, Genesis 21:33, and Isaac built an altar there after God said to him, 'Do not be afraid, for I am with you,' Genesis 26:24. More pointedly, when famine struck in Isaac's day God had told him, 'Do not go down to Egypt,' Genesis 26:2. Abraham's own descent into Egypt during a famine had ended in shame, Genesis 12:10-20. Jacob had every reason to hesitate at the border, and God's word, 'Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt,' answers that hesitation directly.

Goshen lay in the eastern delta, good grazing land and somewhat apart from the Egyptian heartland. Joseph's coaching in Genesis 46:33-34 uses Egyptian prejudice to secure that location. 'All shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians,' just as eating with Hebrews was detestable to them, Genesis 43:32, and as Israel's sacrifices would be, Exodus 8:26. The family's occupation would keep them in a region of their own, preserving their identity.

Pharaoh's question about Jacob's age, Genesis 47:8, is courteous interest in a very old man. Egyptian texts often speak of one hundred and ten years as the ideal span of life, the age at which Joseph himself dies, Genesis 50:26. Jacob at one hundred and thirty had passed it, yet he calls his years 'few and hard.'

The famine measures of Genesis 47:13-26 reflect the logic of a grain economy under royal control. The people pay first with money, then livestock, then land and labour. The fifth of the harvest matches the fifth collected during the years of plenty, Genesis 41:34. The exemption for priests fits what is known of the large temple estates of Egypt. The reference to 'the district of Rameses,' Genesis 47:11, uses a place name associated with the later city of Exodus 1:11, which many take as a later scribe's updating of the name so that readers would know the place.
context.canonical:
The descent into Egypt was foretold long before it happened. God told Abram that his descendants would be 'strangers in a land that is not their own,' enslaved and afterward brought out with possessions, Genesis 15:13-16. This passage is the first step of that prophecy. Exodus picks up exactly where it leaves off: the seventy who went down, Exodus 1:5, 'were fruitful and increased rapidly,' Exodus 1:7, echoing Genesis 47:27.

Israel remembered the descent in its worship. Every farmer bringing firstfruits was to say, 'My father was a wandering Aramean, and he went down to Egypt few in number and lived there and became a great nation,' Deuteronomy 26:5, the very promise of Genesis 46:3. Moses reminded Israel that 'Your fathers went down to Egypt, seventy in all,' and that God had made them 'as numerous as the stars in the sky,' Deuteronomy 10:22. Psalm 105:23-24 sings the same history.

The New Testament takes up three strands. Stephen counts the family who went down as seventy five, Acts 7:14, following the Greek Old Testament, which the BSB footnote on Genesis 46:27 notes. Hebrews draws on the end of the passage: 'By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph's sons and worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff,' Hebrews 11:21, following the Greek reading of Genesis 47:31. Hebrews also gathers Jacob's confession that his life was a sojourn into its portrait of the patriarchs as 'strangers and exiles on the earth,' Hebrews 11:13.

Most strikingly, Matthew applies the pattern of going down to Egypt and being called out to Jesus. When the child is taken to Egypt and returns, Matthew says this fulfilled 'Out of Egypt I called My Son,' Matthew 2:15, quoting Hosea 11:1. The family's descent begins a story that the Son of God would one day live through Himself.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wrote for a people who knew what came next: slavery, the exodus and the wilderness. He wanted them to know that the descent into Egypt was not a mistake to be regretted or a detour from God's plan. It happened at God's word, with God's promise to go with them and to bring them back, Genesis 46:3-4. The long years in Egypt, including the bitter ones, belonged within the covenant.

He also wanted Israel to know their roots by name. The list of seventy tells every later Israelite that his clan goes back to one of these men, and it records the covenant seed at the moment it was smallest, so that its later growth could be seen as God's work, Exodus 1:7.

Finally, Moses shows Israel how to live as a people between promises. Jacob blesses the most powerful king on earth and calls his own life a sojourn, Genesis 47:9. He lives seventeen years in comfort in Goshen, yet his last concern is to be buried in Canaan, Genesis 47:29-30. Israel was to hold Egypt's provision loosely and the land of promise tightly, living where God put them while hoping for what God had sworn.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes the settlement of a family and the economic measures of an Egyptian administration. It does not prescribe a pattern of government or commend the concentration of land in a ruler's hands. Joseph's famine policy is recorded as what he did, and readers must weigh it with care rather than treat it as a blueprint.

Several things do carry forward. Jacob's worship before a journey, Genesis 46:1, models seeking God before great decisions, especially ones that seem to depart from the way God has led before. God's word, 'I will go down with you,' Genesis 46:4, is a promise to the patriarchs, but its substance is repeated for all God's people: 'I am with you always, even to the end of the age,' Matthew 28:20. And Jacob's insistence on being buried in the land of promise models a hope that sits lightly to present comfort. Believers are 'foreigners and exiles,' 1 Peter 2:11, who live faithfully where they are placed while longing for 'a better country,' Hebrews 11:16.

debates.question: How should we assess Joseph's policy of acquiring the people's land and persons for Pharaoh?

views.label: Wise and life saving stewardship
views.case: Joseph keeps a whole population alive through years of famine, and the people themselves say, 'You have saved our lives,' Genesis 47:25. He gives seed for sowing and leaves four fifths of the harvest to the farmers, Genesis 47:24, a rate many readers judge to be moderate. The narrator presents him as the provider God raised up.

views.label: A troubling concentration of power
views.case: Others note the irony that Joseph turns free Egyptians into Pharaoh's servants, Genesis 47:21, and that the same state machinery will later enslave Israel, Exodus 1:11. The narrator records it without comment, and the contrast with Israel's growth in Goshen, Genesis 47:27, may be a quiet critique.

views.label: Faithful service within a fallen system
views.case: A third view holds both together. Joseph served his master faithfully and saved lives, which Scripture commends, while the system he served was Pharaoh's, not God's. The text lets both the rescue and the cost be seen.

debates.bearing: The narrative does not make Joseph a villain; the saved people call him their saviour. But it lets the reader see that a centralised power, however rescuing at first, can become the instrument of oppression when a king arises who does not know Joseph, Exodus 1:8.

debates.question: Did Jacob bow at the head of his bed or lean on the top of his staff, Genesis 47:31?

views.label: The head of his bed
views.case: The traditional Hebrew text reads mittah, bed. It fits the scene of a dying man and anticipates Genesis 48:2, where Israel sits up in bed. Most English versions follow it, as the BSB does.

views.label: The top of his staff
views.case: The same Hebrew consonants can be read matteh, staff, and the Septuagint read them so. Hebrews 11:21 follows the Greek. The staff was part of Jacob's story: 'with only my staff I came across the Jordan,' Genesis 32:10.

debates.bearing: The difference lies in the vowels, which were added long after the consonants were written. Either way the verse describes an act of worship at the end of a life of pilgrimage, and Hebrews rightly calls it faith.

debates.question: Were seventy or seventy five of Jacob's family counted as going to Egypt?

views.label: Seventy
views.case: The Hebrew text of Genesis 46:27, Exodus 1:5 and Deuteronomy 10:22 all give seventy, counting Jacob's direct descendants with Joseph and his two sons.

views.label: Seventy five
views.case: The Septuagint of Genesis 46:27 gives seventy five, apparently including further descendants of Joseph, as the BSB footnote explains. Stephen, speaking to Greek speaking Jews, follows that reckoning, Acts 7:14.

debates.bearing: The two figures count different groups, not contradictory events. Stephen's point is the same as Moses': God brought a small family into Egypt and made them a nation.

study.originalLanguages:
God's promise in Genesis 46:4 is built on two emphatic pronouns: 'I, I will go down with you to Egypt, and I, I will bring you up.' The second clause adds the intensive Hebrew construction of the infinitive with the finite verb, 'bringing up I will bring you up,' which the BSB renders 'I will surely bring you back.' The verb alah, to go up, is the verb of the exodus: God later says He has come down 'to bring them up out of that land,' Exodus 3:8. The promise pairs God's going down with Jacob and His bringing up of Israel, and both halves are His own action.

In Genesis 46:28 Jacob sends Judah ahead 'to get directions,' the verb yarah in its causative form, to point out or teach. It is the root from which torah, instruction, comes. The word is ordinary here, but it gives Judah the role of the one who shows the way, and it continues his emergence as leader.

When Joseph meets his father in verse 29, the BSB says he 'presented himself to him.' The Hebrew uses the passive form of the verb to see, 'he appeared to him,' the same form used again and again when God appears to the patriarchs: 'the LORD appeared to Abram,' Genesis 12:7, and to Isaac, Genesis 26:2 and 26:24. The narrator uses a word of theophany for a son's arrival. It is not that Joseph is divine, but that his appearing to the father who thought him dead has the weight of a revelation.

The 'detestable' of Genesis 46:34 is toevah, a strong word for what is abhorrent or ritually offensive. Genesis uses it only of Egyptian attitudes, here and in Genesis 43:32, and Exodus 8:26 applies it to Israel's sacrifices in Egyptian eyes. Later the law and the prophets turn the word around and use it for what is detestable to the LORD.

Jacob's answer to Pharaoh, Genesis 47:9, uses the noun megurim, sojournings, twice, as the BSB footnote notes: 'the years of my sojournings.' It comes from gur, to live as a resident alien, the verb the brothers use when they say they have come 'to live in the land for a time,' Genesis 47:4, and that described Abram going down to Egypt 'to live there for a while,' Genesis 12:10. God had called Canaan 'the land where you are residing,' literally the land of your sojournings, Genesis 17:8. Jacob sees his whole life, in Canaan and in Egypt, as a sojourn.

Finally, Jacob asks Joseph in Genesis 47:29 to show him 'kindness and faithfulness,' chesed and emet. The pair was used of God's faithfulness to Abraham, Genesis 24:27, and of God's dealings with Jacob himself, Genesis 32:10, and it becomes the heart of God's self description, 'abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness,' Exodus 34:6. Jacob asks his son to deal with him in the way God has dealt with them all.

typology.type: Israel's descent into Egypt and promised return, Genesis 46:3-4
typology.fulfillment: God sends Israel down to Egypt with a promise to bring him up again, and the exodus fulfils it. Matthew sees the same pattern in Jesus, taken to Egypt as a child and brought out, 'Out of Egypt I called My Son,' Matthew 2:15, quoting Hosea 11:1. Jesus relives Israel's story as the true Son. The escalation is that Israel came out of Egypt only to fail in the wilderness, while Jesus goes through the wilderness and remains faithful, Matthew 4:1-11, and His exodus through death brings His people out of a greater bondage.

typology.type: Joseph, who kept a starving world alive, Genesis 47:13-25
typology.fulfillment: The Egyptians say to Joseph, 'You have saved our lives,' Genesis 47:25. Jesus says, 'I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger,' John 6:35. The type is instructive most of all where it falls short. Joseph's bread cost the Egyptians their money, their herds, their land and their freedom. Christ's bread is given freely: 'you without money, come, buy, and eat,' Isaiah 55:1. Joseph's provision made people servants of Pharaoh; Christ's makes servants into sons.

typology.type: Jacob the sojourner who blesses the king, Genesis 47:7-10
typology.fulfillment: A landless alien twice blesses the ruler of Egypt, and Hebrews states the principle: 'the lesser is blessed by the greater,' Hebrews 7:7. Jacob carries the promise that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham's line, Genesis 12:3, and Paul says that promise foretold the gospel to the Gentiles, Galatians 3:8. God's people, 'foreigners and exiles,' 1 Peter 2:11, carry that blessing to the nations in Christ, the true seed through whom it comes.

typology.type: Jacob's charge to be buried in the land, Genesis 47:29-30
typology.fulfillment: Jacob refuses to let Egypt be his final resting place and binds Joseph by oath to carry him to Canaan. Hebrews says the patriarchs 'died in faith, without having received the things they were promised,' Hebrews 11:13, longing for 'a better country, a heavenly one,' Hebrews 11:16. Jacob's hope was for a grave in the promised land; the gospel's hope is for the grave itself to be emptied, secured by Christ's resurrection. The type points beyond itself.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through God's promise of presence. 'I will go down with you to Egypt,' Genesis 46:4, is God's pledge not to remain behind in Canaan but to accompany His people into a foreign land. In the incarnation that promise takes flesh. 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and the child is named Immanuel, 'God with us,' Matthew 1:23. God did not merely go down with His people into exile; in His Son He took on their condition, 'taking the form of a servant,' Philippians 2:7. And the risen Christ repeats the promise of Beersheba to His disciples: 'surely I am with you always,' Matthew 28:20.

It leads to Christ through the pattern of Israel's story. Israel went down to Egypt as a son and was called out, Hosea 11:1. Matthew sees Jesus as the one who relives that history, taken into Egypt and brought out again, Matthew 2:15. Jesus is the faithful Israel, the Son in whom the nation's calling is finally fulfilled. The seventy who went down were the whole of Israel in seed form; Jesus is Israel in person.

It leads to Christ through contrast with Joseph's provision. Joseph saved lives, and the Egyptians said so, Genesis 47:25. But his salvation came at a price the people paid themselves: silver, livestock, land and liberty. Christ gives the bread of life without price, John 6:35, and He pays the cost Himself. Those who received Joseph's grain became Pharaoh's servants; those who receive Christ receive 'adoption as sons,' Galatians 4:5.

It leads to Christ through blessing to the nations. Jacob, a frail old man with nothing but a promise, blesses Pharaoh twice. The promise to Abraham was that all nations would be blessed through his seed, and Paul says Scripture 'foretold the gospel to Abraham,' Galatians 3:8. In Jacob's hands the blessing reaches a Gentile king for a moment. In Christ it reaches the world.

Finally, Jacob's last request looks toward resurrection. He wants his bones carried to the land of promise, because he believes God's word about it will outlast his death. The New Testament says the patriarchs died in faith, welcoming the promises from afar, Hebrews 11:13. Their hope rested on a God who is not ashamed to be called their God, Hebrews 11:16, and that hope is made sure in the One who rose from the dead as the firstfruits of all who sleep. The links are real, but they are links of pattern and promise; the wagons, the land sales and the list of names are not allegories of Christ, and should not be read as such.
study.god:
The God of these chapters speaks only once, in a single night vision, Genesis 46:2-4, and everything else unfolds under that word. His self introduction, 'I am God, the God of your father,' ties Him to Isaac and Abraham before Him. He is not a new god for a new land but the same God who has kept this family for three generations. His covenant faithfulness is the backbone of the passage.

He is the God who goes with His people. The promise 'I will go down with you' answers a fear that must have been real: that to leave Canaan was to leave God's presence and forfeit His promise. The God of Genesis is not bound to a territory. He met Jacob at Bethel as he fled, Genesis 28:15, and He goes with him into Egypt. Isaiah later hears the same promise for exiles: 'When you pass through the waters, I will be with you,' Isaiah 43:2.

He is the God who keeps His promise in His own way and time. The great nation of Genesis 12:2 will be made 'there,' in Egypt, Genesis 46:3, not in Canaan. The land promise remains, but its fulfilment is postponed, and God had already told Abram why, Genesis 15:13-16. God is not in a hurry, and He is not thwarted. The family grows most in the place that seems farthest from the promise, Genesis 47:27.

He is the God who blesses the nations through His chosen people. Jacob's blessing of Pharaoh, Genesis 47:7 and 47:10, is a small enactment of Genesis 12:3. Pharaoh has received Abraham's seed kindly, and Abraham's seed blesses him. The same God is at work in Joseph's administration keeping Egypt and Canaan alive through the famine, so His care reaches beyond Israel even while it centres on Israel.

The passage also holds a tension. God brings Israel into Egypt, and Egypt will become a house of bondage. The God who says 'Do not be afraid' knows what lies ahead, Genesis 15:13. His presence does not guarantee an easy path, but it does guarantee the end: 'I will surely bring you back.' When the bondage comes, 'God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,' Exodus 2:24.

For worship, Jacob gives the pattern. He sacrifices before setting out, Genesis 46:1, and he bows in worship as he prepares to die, Genesis 47:31. A life lived between God's promise and its fulfilment is framed by worship of the God who goes with His people and brings them home.

crossReferences.note: In a famine God told Isaac, 'Do not go down to Egypt.' The contrast explains Jacob's pause at Beersheba and the need for a fresh word. Going down to Egypt was not wrong in itself, but it was not to be done without God's direction, and in Genesis 46:3 that direction is given.

God foretold that Abram's descendants would be strangers in a foreign land, enslaved and then brought out with possessions. Genesis 46 begins the fulfilment. The descent that looks like an interruption of the promise is itself part of what God announced beforehand.

At Bethel God promised Jacob, 'I am with you... and I will bring you back to this land.' Genesis 46:4 renews the same promise at the start of a far longer journey. The God who went with Jacob to Paddan-aram now goes with his whole family to Egypt.

Exodus opens with the same formula as Genesis 46:8, 'These are the names of the sons of Israel who went to Egypt,' and the same number, seventy. It then reports the growth promised in Genesis 46:3, tying the two books into one story.

Israel's confession at the offering of firstfruits: 'he went down to Egypt few in number and lived there and became a great nation.' The worshipper repeats Genesis 46:3 as a fulfilled promise, turning family history into a creed.

'The lesser is blessed by the greater.' Applied to Genesis 47:7-10, the principle reveals who truly holds the greater standing in that audience. Jacob has no land and no army, but he bears the blessing of God, and Pharaoh receives it from him.

The patriarchs acknowledged that they were 'strangers and exiles on the earth.' Jacob's description of his life as a sojourn, Genesis 47:9, is one of the clearest examples. Faith lives in the present as a resident alien, because its home lies in what God has promised.

Jacob 'worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff,' following the Greek reading of Genesis 47:31. Hebrews treats the dying patriarch's worship, and his blessing of Joseph's sons, as an act of faith looking beyond death to God's promise.

Joseph, dying in Egypt, repeats his father's hope: 'God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land.' He too asks for his bones to be carried out. The charge of Genesis 47:29-30 becomes the family's lasting confession of hope.

Jesus is taken to Egypt and brought out, fulfilling 'Out of Egypt I called My Son.' The descent of Genesis 46 and the exodus it anticipates become a pattern the Son of God lives out, marking Him as the true Israel.

'Surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.' The promise of presence God gave Jacob at Beersheba, Genesis 46:4, is spoken by the risen Christ to His people as they go out into all nations.

study.oneStory:
The promise of Genesis began with a blessing on humanity, 'Be fruitful and multiply,' Genesis 1:28, and after the fall it narrowed to one family through whom all families would be blessed, Genesis 12:3. By Genesis 46 that family numbers seventy. It is small, threatened by famine, and about to leave the land it was promised. These chapters show how God keeps His word in unexpected places.

The passage answers a question the patriarchal story has been raising: how can a family of wandering herdsmen become a great nation? The answer is Egypt. In Goshen the blessing of creation comes alive again, for the Israelites 'became fruitful and increased greatly in number,' Genesis 47:27. What Adam's race was told to do, and what the flood interrupted, God now brings to pass in Abraham's seed.

It also sets up the next great act of the story. Exodus begins with these names and this growth, and then with a king who did not know Joseph. The land that sheltered Israel becomes the land that enslaves them, and out of that slavery God will bring them with a mighty hand. The promise 'I will surely bring you back' becomes the exodus, the defining act of salvation in the Old Testament.

The New Testament shows that this pattern reaches its goal in Jesus. The Son of God goes down into Egypt and is called out. He goes down further still, into death, and is brought up again. In Him God's promise to be with His people becomes God dwelling among them in the flesh. And in Him the blessing Jacob gave to Pharaoh reaches all the nations.

The story ends where Jacob's hope pointed. He did not want his bones to stay in Egypt, because he trusted God's promise of the land. The final chapters of Scripture show that promise enlarged beyond anything Jacob could have pictured: a new heaven and a new earth, where 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3. The sojourners will be home at last, and God, who went down with His people into Egypt, will dwell with them for ever.

quiz.q: What does God tell Jacob in the vision at Beersheba?

options.text: Do not be afraid to go to Egypt, for I will go with you and surely bring you back.
options.note: God promises His presence in exile and a future return.

options.text: Stay in Canaan and do not go down to Egypt.
options.note: The opposite; God sanctions the descent and even blesses it.

options.text: Egypt will become the permanent home of his descendants.
options.note: God promises to bring them back, not to leave them there forever.

options.text: Joseph has died and Jacob should mourn.
options.note: God speaks of blessing and return, and Joseph is very much alive.

quiz.q: Why does the passage carefully list the seventy who went down to Egypt?

options.text: To record the covenant seed that will grow into the promised nation.
options.note: The roll of names ties this family to the great nation of the exodus.

options.text: To show that the family was too large to feed.
options.note: The list marks the covenant seed, not a feeding problem; Joseph provides for them.

options.text: Simply to fill space in the narrative.
options.note: The genealogy has real theological weight, linking the household to a nation.

options.text: To prove the brothers had abandoned Jacob.
options.note: The opposite; the whole family travels together to Joseph.

quiz.q: What is striking about Jacob's meeting with Pharaoh?

options.text: The aged, landless patriarch blesses the mighty Pharaoh, the greater blessing the lesser.
options.note: Jacob blesses Pharaoh twice, quietly signaling whose God is sovereign.

options.text: Pharaoh refuses to let the family settle.
options.note: Pharaoh generously grants them the best of the land.

options.text: Jacob demands a throne of his own.
options.note: Jacob seeks no power; he blesses Pharaoh and speaks humbly of his hard years.

options.text: Jacob hides that his sons are shepherds.
options.note: Their shepherding is openly stated and leads to their settling in Goshen.

quiz.q: How do the Egyptians respond to Joseph's provision during the famine?

options.text: They say, you have saved our lives, and become Pharaoh's servants.
options.note: Joseph's administration keeps a starving nation alive.

options.text: They revolt against Pharaoh and Joseph.
options.note: There is no revolt; they willingly sell land for food and thank Joseph.

options.text: They flee Egypt entirely.
options.note: They stay and receive seed to sow under Joseph's new arrangement.

options.text: They accuse Joseph of hoarding grain unjustly.
options.note: They credit him with saving their lives, not with injustice.

quiz.q: Why does Jacob make Joseph swear to bury him with his fathers, not in Egypt?

options.text: His hope rests in the land of promise, looking beyond death to God's covenant.
options.note: Jacob's dying request is an act of covenant faith.

options.text: He dislikes Egyptian burial customs.
options.note: The real issue is the promised land, not merely custom.

options.text: He wants to punish his sons for settling in Egypt.
options.note: It is faith in the promise, not punishment, that drives his request.

options.text: He no longer believes God's promises.
options.note: His request is precisely an expression of faith in those promises.

questions: Before the biggest move of his life, Jacob stopped to worship and heard God say, do not be afraid. What decision are you facing that you need to bring to God before taking a step?
God promised to go down to Egypt with Jacob. Where do you need to trust that God goes with you into an unfamiliar or unwanted season?
A frail old man blessed the most powerful ruler on earth. How does this reshape your sense of where real significance and authority come from?
Joseph used his position to keep others alive. How might God be calling you to use your resources or influence to provide for people in need?
Jacob died looking toward a promise he had not yet received. What promises of God are you holding onto that reach beyond what you can see now?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew counts the family as seventy; some Greek witnesses read seventy-five, the figure Stephen cites in Acts 7:14, reflecting a slightly different way of counting Joseph's descendants.
The reading that Joseph reduced the people to servitude follows the Samaritan, Greek, and Latin; the traditional Hebrew reads that he removed the people to the cities.
Israel bowed at the head of his bed follows the Hebrew; the Greek reads that he worshiped leaning on the top of his staff, the wording quoted in Hebrews 11:21.
